messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: benefit of using fma?
parts:
Hi!

What is the benefit of using the function fma? If I look at the C++ code it translates to, it is nothing else than writing down a*b+c... is it easier to derive the partial derivatives?

I am fine with using these special functions, but as these do not increase readability of my code this case is from my naive view not really a gain.

Many thanks for some insight on this.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] benefit of using fma?
parts:
For now, the only advantage is that it saves a bit on the
partial derivatives. There's a bit less memory involved
and it's a bit faster.

We also have it in place on the C++ side so that we
have full coverage of the basic C++ math libs. See:

http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/math/fma

It should probably be recoded to call the built-in
library fma() code, which can sometimes be compiled
down to faster machine code. fma() is technically part
of the TR1 libraries, but it doesn't look like it got
added to the main C++ distributions until C++11.

Does anyone know more about its availability? I'd be happy
to drop in a faster version if one were available without
using C++11. (We're trying to avoid C++11 until R supports
it, but may give that up at some point, especially if
RStudio moves over to a clang++ and C++11 basis.

- Bob
